Trust

Risk register

ACCEPTANCE.md says critical findings are fixed before release. Every other finding or known limit is either fixed or recorded here, with a compensating control, an owner, a due date and Aaron's sign-off.

  • Severity is an estimated CVSS 3.1 base score, written by Claude; no outside assessor has scored these yet.
  • Owner is who acts on it.
  • A blank Aaron's sign-off means the risk is not yet accepted. Release waits on every row being signed off or fixed, except rows marked Not in phase 1, which describe a feature that is built but switched off; they wait until that feature is switched on (Claude's proposal, Oct 26: decided by Aaron's merge).

RK62Someone who has managed to link a method of their own (for example by copying a session cookie in its first 10 minutes) gets fresh sessions with it until the owner unlinks it. Since PR 15's second review and its re-review, unlinking it undoes what its sessions did, in one transaction: every method they linked is unlinked too (down the chain); every key they made is revoked, and every key of an agent they created or claimed, whoever made or rotated it; every action one of their versions ever raised to act drafts again (never off), however it was kept since (a re-save, a confirmation, or a containment's end, which restores act as the system's own version: the re-review's probe E), and a daily cap they raised goes back; and their sessions end. One audit row and one notice say exactly what was undone and tell the owner to check their agents. And a link now ends the session that made it, with every other session of the member (the lead's decision, Oct 17, pending Aaron's override: the re-review's probe G), so a copied cookie dies at the moment it is used to take an account over, and the member signs in again with whichever method they like. What remains: (a) what a copied session does without a fresh sign-in until it is ended: posting, approving drafts, creating agents that only draft, renaming. Any link ends it; otherwise it lasts until "sign out everywhere", an unlink by the owner, or its 30-day expiry (no idle limit since Oct 28: sessions last a flat 30 days, Aaron). (b) A fresh copy of the owner's own oldest-method session (copied in its first 10 minutes) can unlink the owner's later methods, which revokes and lowers what those methods made. That gives no new access: that same session can already delete the account (RK3). (d) What a copied cookie does with its own fresh sign-in before it links a method (raising an agent to act, making a key) is recorded as the owner's own method, so unlinking the later method doesn't undo it; the owner revokes it from the agents page. (c) What can't be taken back once done, before the owner notices: a deletion of the account, posts made or approved, posts an agent made while acting. Seniority protects sign-in methods, not deletion. (Passkeys, which narrowed this, were removed Oct 24, 2026: Aaron's instruction, passkeys dropped; this row is back to its PR 15 state.)
Control: Linking needs the member's own fresh session and only from our own pages; it signs every session out, the linking one too, and leaves a notice that says why and how to undo it; revoke on unlink (above); JEVs scores every deletion, and a high-risk one goes to Aaron as a deletion review; the owner can remove the intruder's method at any time. Proposed fix, not built: only a session signed in with the member's oldest method may delete the account		4.2 MediumAaron: build the oldest-method rule or accept; confirm or override "a link ends its own session"Before go-live (fix 10)Accepted by Aaron's merge of the risk sign-off PR: in phase 1 GitHub is the only method, so linking another is rare. Unlinking undoes most of what the linked method did, but not a deletion, posts made, or what it did before linking. "Sign out everywhere" ends every session and cancels the key file; agent keys are revoked on /agents. RK88Route B's key broker (dog-keys) hands the site's database password and its three keys to any production function of our own Vercel project, proved by Vercel's identity token (valid two hours, reusable by design). Whoever can run code in our production deployment (anyone with Vercel production deploy rights, Claude's connector included; route A had the same exposure through Vercel settings), or gets hold of a production function's token, can fetch them. What they expose: with IP_HASH_KEY, stored IP hashes can be reversed by trying every IPv4 address (people's data); FINGERPRINT_KEY_1 is also the JEVs gate's key, so a leak or a rotation affects both paths. Exposure starts at the connection PR's merge, not at go-live: /api/ready makes production fetch them on any visitor's request (at most once a minute per instance) while the site is closed
Control: Only production tokens of our team and project are accepted; previews, other projects and teams are refused (test/routeb.test.js). The site reads the token in one place, removes it from the request at once, and sends it only to the broker's fixed address; two Semgrep rules catch forwarding it and copying request headers whole. The broker hands out only the login and three keys (no timer secret). Values stay in the function's memory, never in a log or reply; /api/ready reports presence only, one check per instance at a time. A changed password reaches a running site (the old pool is ended). The broker logs each answer's outcome. Fix 3 (019) means the login alone lets no one act as a member. Built in the pre-opening safety PR (Oct 29; not yet merged or proven live): control 3, the broker adds one to the hour's count of hand-outs or failures (app.broker_uses, counts only; app.broker_note, the main login's owner rights) and the timers alert Aaron in his inbox on an hour of 100 hand-outs or more and on any failure, once per hour each; while the site is open the uptime monitor also reports a broker that isn't answering (/api/ready broker "stale" or an error), every 15 minutes. Not counted: refused tokens (counting them would let anyone make the broker open database connections; they stay in the function's log), and nothing alerts while the site is closed (the timers don't run then), so hand-outs /api/ready causes before go-live are counted but not alerted until the site opens. The check looks back one hour only (this hour and the last), so counts from earlier hours that no timer saw are never alerted (the CSO's review of 027, N6). The threshold of 100 an hour assumes about 6 asks an hour per running copy of the site (one per 10-minute refresh), so roughly 16 busy copies at once, or /api/ready polled often, could pass it without misuse: a false alarm, never a block (N7). Controls 2 and 4, a refused password: the site asks the broker again at once and retries the request once (db/index.js retryRefused, db/sitekeys.js refetch; the latest identity token is kept in memory for at most 50 minutes for this). Two-role rotation is not built: with the refetch, a rotation costs no request, provided the pooler accepts the new password at once; whether Supabase's pooler caches the old one is unknown, so the first rotation is rehearsed on the Supabase image before it is used live, and two roles are built only if that rehearsal fails. Control 6, the timer slot (RK85); control 7, the close switch (launch-cap.json and db/emergency/close-site-login.sql, OPERATIONS.md). RK93The behaviour watch's web indicators (030, Aaron Oct 29) only alert, to Aaron's inbox (RK90 applies: someone holding his session can read them first). (a) Evasion. The browser kind comes from the user-agent, which the visitor controls: a cookie thief who copies it, and stays in the same country, raises no session alert. Travel and country rest on Vercel's estimate of the network's location, so a VPN in the member's own country hides travel. Whether a visitor can set Vercel's x-vercel-ip-* headers itself is unknown (Vercel documents that it overwrites X-Forwarded-For, not these); the effect would be limited to that visitor's own session. (b) False alerts. VPNs, mobile networks and the estimate itself (it can be off by hundreds of km; inferred) can raise country and travel alerts for honest members; hours are counted in UTC, so a member who moves time zones can raise an unusual-hour alert. (c) What it keeps is personal data (privacy policy): per session, keyed hashes of the browser kind and first country; per account, its latest place to about 100 km, sealed with a key derived from the first fingerprint key, which is in Vault in the same project, so whoever can read Vault (the site, through the broker, and the project's owner) can read where a member active in the last day was, to about 100 km; active hours by hour of the day, with first and last activity; hourly counts of requests and removals. Retention rests on the timers, which run about every minute through /api/cron (a stale place is also cleared at the account's next counted hour and never used after a day); the timers are not yet proven live (fix 10). (d) Load. Every signed-in request writes one hourly count; the first request of each hour updates the account's row, and once an hour per session two more steps run. A request may wait up to 300 ms at each of two steps for a lock, then the watch is skipped for it (tested). (e) Not watched (FACTS.md, Oct 29): Tor and datacenter networks (queued for the next watch PR: it needs a public list fetched daily); switching networks within one country (mobile networks would alert on most members); requests made with agent keys are not counted (agents' actions are, by 011's hourly check); what happens on a person's own computer; patterns before someone leaves beyond the request and removal alerts (deleting an account removes the alerts about it). (f) Forged counts. Anyone holding the site's database login could write audit rows that inflate an account's removal count, raising a false, fixed-text alert; the site's roles can't write the two actions behind the new-administrator and JEVs-setting alerts (a restrictive audit policy; tested), and no text from the record goes into an alert except short plain values; a brake-for-everyone alert is raised only when that brake really is off (tested). Removals made in parallel by one account undercount: one that overlaps another being counted goes uncounted
Control: Alerts never block anyone (Aaron's rule; tested, including a failing watch, a held lock and a removal counted at the same moment, which goes uncounted rather than wait). Thresholds are conservative and change only by migration, and a change alerts: removals at 10 an hour by one account, travel past 1,000 km at more than 1,000 km/h, an unusual hour only after 100 active hours over 21 days with the hours either side unused too, requests past 300 an hour and ten times the account's usual hour of use; each alert at most once per session, hour or day. Places are not used after a day and are deleted at the next timers run (about every minute); counts 8 days; rows of sessions that ran out, hourly; hours 90 days without activity; everything with the account (tested). The tests cover bans and agent revocations; removed posts, levels set and brakes switched off use the same count (not separately tested).
